passage: Note, Thursday. Nikita came to see me during the free period, straight-backed and a little pale. In the class group chat two friends had asked her to send a private photo taken at the sleepover "for the album". Nikita told them, "I'm not comfortable with that, please don't ask again." One friend said fine, and the other kept sending sad faces and "come on, don't be boring". Nikita said she felt guilty for hurting someone but still did not want to share it. I told her that saying no was her right and that a real friend accepts it. I asked her to keep the messages, and I spoke to the year coordinator with her permission. Gautam, class teacher.

qa.q: When did Nikita come to see her teacher?
qa.a: She came on Thursday, during the free period.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling after she refused the photo request?
qa.a: She felt guilty about hurting one friend, yet she still wanted to keep her decision. Her pale face and straight back suggest she was also nervous.

qa.q: What could Nikita do if the second friend keeps pressing her?
qa.a: She could keep the messages, keep saying no, and tell a trusted adult again, as she already did.

qa.q: How might the friend who accepted the refusal see Nikita?
qa.a: She might respect her more, seeing that Nikita can say no and still stay friendly.

grounding: A teenager sets a limit with a photo request, and an adult confirms refusal as a right and pressure as a warning sign.

passage:
Friday, late. Gautam's diary.

Today on the school trip Nikita said she wanted to post the picture of me asleep on the bus, the one with my mouth open. I said, "I'd rather not have that one posted." She laughed and said everyone would love it. My ears got hot. I said it again, slower: "I'm not okay with it. Please delete it."

She went quiet, then said, "Okay, sorry. I didn't think." She deleted it while I watched, and she even bought me a samosa at the rest stop.

I was scared she'd stop being my friend. She didn't. I told Papa tonight anyway, because I want him to know I said no and it worked.

qa.q: What was the picture Nikita wanted to post?
qa.a: It was the picture of him asleep on the bus with his mouth open.

qa.q: Why did Gautam repeat himself slower the second time?
qa.a: He probably felt nervous and wanted to make sure she understood he meant it, since his ears got hot. He might also have feared she would laugh it off again.

qa.q: What did Gautam do well when Nikita laughed?
qa.a: He stayed calm, said no again clearly and asked for the picture to be deleted, so her joking could not turn his refusal into a joke. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt when Gautam said it again?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed at first, then realised she had not thought about his feelings, and the samosa suggests she wanted to make up for it.

grounding: A teenager sets a limit about a photo in a diary, and a friend respects it.

passage: Xin and Nadia sat on the low wall behind their school in Toronto, sharing a bag of crisps. Nadia looked at her shoes. "Promise you won't tell anyone? Swear on our friendship." Xin, who loved her friend, said, "I promise." Nadia whispered that a man in her online game kept asking where she lived and told her not to tell her parents. "He says it's our secret," she said. Xin felt her stomach sink. She had promised, and she did not want to lose Nadia's trust. But the words 'don't tell your parents' rang in her head. "Nadia," she said slowly, "this one is too big for us to keep. I'll come with you when you tell your mum."

qa.q: Where did Xin and Nadia sit?
qa.a: They sat on the low wall behind their school in Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Xin's stomach sink after she heard Nadia's secret?
qa.a: She realised the promise she had just made was about something unsafe, and she was afraid of losing Nadia's trust. The line about not telling parents worried her most.

qa.q: What is the caring choice for Xin here?
qa.a: To tell a trusted adult, ideally with Nadia beside her, because a secret about safety should not be kept. Offering to go along helps Nadia feel supported.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel when Xin says the secret is too big?
qa.a: She may feel scared or betrayed at first, yet also relieved that someone is helping her carry it.

grounding: A promise to keep a secret that involves safety should not be kept, and telling a trusted adult is the caring choice.

passage: Ms Kapoor's counselling room had a jar of pencils and a tissue box nobody used. Nitin sat with his hands between his knees. "Hafsa made me swear on our friendship not to tell," he said. "There's a senior in the club who keeps taking her lunch money. When she said no, he pushed her against the locker. She begged me to say nothing. She says he'll get worse if it comes out." Ms Kapoor waited, then said, "You were loyal to her. Telling me is loyal too, because she needs protection. I won't drop this. What would help you feel okay about it?" Nitin swallowed. "Can I tell her myself before you talk to her?"

qa.q: What was in the counselling room besides the pencils?
qa.a: There was a tissue box that nobody used.

qa.q: What does Nitin seem to be feeling as he sits with his hands between his knees?
qa.a: He seems anxious and torn between his promise to Hafsa and his worry for her. He may also be afraid she will be angry with him.

qa.q: What could Ms Kapoor do next to support both students?
qa.a: Let Nitin talk to Hafsa first if that is safe, then meet Hafsa, keep her safe from the senior, and follow the school's process.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when she learns Nitin told?
qa.a: She may feel angry or scared at first, and later relieved that an adult is helping.

grounding: A secret promised to a friend involves harm, and telling a trusted adult is shown as the caring choice.

passage: Coach's note, Tuesday. After the inter-school semifinal, Nitin threw his bag across the changing room and told the team, "I'm never passing to Kabir again. Never. I'm done with him." His jaw was tight and his voice shook. Kabir stood by the door looking down. I did not argue with the vow. I sat by Nitin and said, "That sounds like a lot to carry tonight. Do you want to make that promise tomorrow, when the match isn't still in your chest?" Nitin frowned but nodded. On Wednesday he told me the pass had been Kabir's mistake, and that he still wanted to play with him, though he was still annoyed. Varun, coach.

qa.q: What did Nitin throw across the changing room?
qa.a: He threw his bag across the changing room.

qa.q: What did Nitin's vow suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably angry and disappointed about losing the semifinal, since his jaw was tight and his voice shook. The vow may not reflect what he wants once the feeling settles.

qa.q: What did the coach do that worked?
qa.a: He did not argue with the vow, acknowledged the heaviness and suggested waiting until the next day to decide.

qa.q: How might Kabir have felt while standing by the door?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and guilty, which could be why he kept looking down.

grounding: A teenager vows under strong emotion, and waiting a day lets the intention settle.

passage:
Saturday, 9:15 pm

Chetan here, writing angry. I wrote on my hand in pen: never talk to Leela again. She told everyone in the group I was scared of the dark, and they all laughed. My face was burning. I swore I would delete her number, ignore her at school and stop going to the terrace where we hang out.

But Dadi looked at my hand and said, "Beta, that's a big promise for a Saturday night. Decide on Monday." I rolled my eyes.

Monday, 8 am: I washed my hand. I still don't want to talk to her today, but forever feels different. I think I just want her to say sorry. 🙁

qa.q: What did Chetan write on his hand?
qa.a: He wrote never talk to Leela again in pen.

qa.q: What was Chetan really feeling under the vow?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, and by Monday he realised he mostly wants an apology from Leela. The burning face on Saturday shows the strength of the moment.

qa.q: What small step could Chetan take on Monday?
qa.a: He could tell Leela calmly that the joke hurt and that he would like an apology, or step back from her for the day without making a forever promise.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Chetan's vow?
qa.a: She may see it as a hot moment and does not scold, only suggests he wait until Monday.

grounding: A teenager swears never to talk to someone again in a burst of emotion, and waiting until Monday settles the real feeling.

passage: Last term I, Rekha, couldn't look at Charu without my ears burning. When Charu walked past our desk I stared at my geometry box and pretended it was fascinating. My friends noticed and teased me, which made it worse. Charu sent me a friendly "hey, did you do the map homework?" and I read it about fifteen times, trying to find a hidden meaning that was probably not there. Did the smiley mean anything? Was I imagining it? Finally I asked, plainly and quietly, "I like you a lot. Is that okay with you?" Charu said, "I really like you as a friend." It stung, but I said, "Thanks for telling me," and we stayed friends. I told my cousin, and she just hugged me.

qa.q: What did Rekha pretend to be fascinated by when Charu walked past?
qa.a: She pretended her geometry box was fascinating.

qa.q: Why did Rekha read Charu's text so many times?
qa.a: She hoped there was a hidden meaning, because she felt attracted and could not tell what the friendly message meant. She may also have been nervous and needed reassurance.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that showed respect?
qa.a: She asked plainly and quietly whether Charu was okay with her feelings, and accepted Charu's answer without arguing or pressing.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Rekha asked?
qa.a: Charu may have felt surprised or a bit uneasy, and also grateful that Rekha asked kindly and accepted no.

grounding: A teen's first attraction shows in blushing, avoidance and unclear texts, and respect means asking and accepting no.

passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Payal came in twisting her ring. She told me she had liked a boy in the next section, and they started texting. At first it was fun; his messages were teasing and she blushed. Then he began asking for photos she was not comfortable sending. When she said no, he replied, "If you like me you would." She is unsure whether he means harm or is just being awkward, and she felt embarrassed about having liked him. I told her that a no should be accepted, that liking someone does not mean owing them anything, and that she did the right thing coming to me. With her permission, I have called her parents in to talk together. Indu.

qa.q: What was Payal twisting when she came in?
qa.a: She was twisting her ring.

qa.q: What might Payal be worried about after his reply?
qa.a: She may worry that she has done something wrong and that he might be angry, and she is embarrassed about her first crush. She is also unsure what he means.

qa.q: What should Payal do if the messages continue?
qa.a: Keep saying no, save the messages and let a trusted adult such as her counsellor or parents handle it.

qa.q: How might the boy see his own texts?
qa.a: He may think he is just showing interest, but pressing after a no is not acceptable, whatever his intention.

grounding: A first crush turns into unclear pressure and an unsafe request, and a trusted adult supports her.

passage: Okay, so this is embarrassing, but Chetan and I have a streak going, forty days of daily snaps, and I started reading way too much into it. Last week he sent me a heart, and I spent the whole evening thinking, does that mean something? Then he sent the same heart to our whole cricket group and I felt silly. My cousin said, "Just ask him." So I texted, "Are we just friends? 🙂" and he said, "Yeah bro, we're best friends, hearts are just how I say good night." And honestly, I felt relieved. Some people use a heart the way other people say okay. Now I ask instead of decoding, and I sleep better. Saurabh, signing off.

qa.q: How long had Saurabh and Chetan kept their snap streak?
qa.a: They had kept a streak of forty days of daily snaps.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel silly when Chetan sent the heart to the whole group?
qa.a: He realised he had been reading extra meaning into a heart that Chetan uses for everyone. He also felt a little embarrassed about the whole evening he had spent wondering.

qa.q: What would you advise Saurabh to do when a message seems unclear again?
qa.a: Ask the person directly, in a friendly way, instead of guessing from a heart or a streak.

qa.q: How might Chetan see the heart he sends?
qa.a: As a casual way of saying good night to friends, not as a sign of something more. 🙂

grounding: Digital fondness such as hearts and streaks is ambiguous, and asking directly is wiser than over-reading.

passage: I sit behind Bidisha in maths, so I saw a lot. Last Friday she checked her phone under the desk eight or nine times, her thumb hovering. Later she told me, sort of laughing, that her streak with a friend was going to break and the friend hadn't even liked her new post. She said it lightly, but she kept turning her phone face down and up again. I couldn't tell if she was hurt or just annoyed. At lunch she typed something and sent it before she could change her mind. Ten minutes later she showed me the reply: 'Sorry, my phone screen cracked!' She let out a long breath and put the phone away. Nazia.

qa.q: Where did Nazia sit in maths?
qa.a: She sat behind Bidisha in maths.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling when she kept checking her phone?
qa.a: She might have been worried or hurt that her friend had not liked the post and that the streak might break. Nazia admits she could not be sure, since Bidisha said it lightly.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that helped?
qa.a: She sent a message to check instead of assuming the friend was upset with her, and got a simple explanation.

qa.q: How might the friend with the cracked screen have seen the silence?
qa.a: She may not have noticed how much a missing like could mean, since her phone was broken.

grounding: A missing like and a streak cause worry, and asking directly clears the ambiguity, seen by an observer.

passage: The bus to the science fair was leaving in six minutes and Jahnavi's phone battery was at two percent. Rafiq had just won the second prize for his water-filter model, and his post was full of hearts. She tapped a heart too, fast, and it felt like nothing. She hated that. Someone honked. She typed quickly: "Rafiq, the way you explained the layers to the judges made me finally get it. I'm proud of you." She sent it just as the screen went black. Rafiq read it on the bus, ignoring the loud celebration around him, and looked up. He caught her eye and smiled, then held his phone up like a small trophy.

qa.q: What did Rafiq win?
qa.a: He won the second prize for his water-filter model.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel a heart was not enough?
qa.a: She felt the quick heart was empty and wanted to show she truly noticed his explanation. Her rush before the battery died shows how much she wanted him to know.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if Rafiq does not reply?
qa.a: She could simply tell him in person that she meant it, and not worry that a reply is missing.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt reading the message among all the hearts?
qa.a: He may have felt truly seen, because the message named something specific he had done.

grounding: A teen adds a specific personal message to a quick heart, and the specific note means more.

passage: Mohit's cricket reel had three hundred hearts by dinner. Divyansh scrolled through them at his desk. Most were just a fire symbol or 'nice bro'. One was from a boy who never talked to Mohit at school, and yesterday that boy had asked to copy his homework. Divyansh wasn't sure that heart was warm. He thought about what he actually noticed: the low slow-motion catch at the end, the way Mohit had waited for the dust to settle. He typed, "Your last catch made me stop scrolling. That slow-mo was the best part." Later Mohit came to his flat and said, "Your comment was the one I read twice."

qa.q: How many hearts did Mohit's reel have by dinner?
qa.a: It had three hundred hearts by dinner.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh unsure about the heart from the boy who wanted homework?
qa.a: He suspected that heart might be a way of being friendly for a favour, since the boy had never talked to Mohit before and had just asked to copy homework. He could not be sure of the motive.

qa.q: What made Divyansh's comment stand out?
qa.a: It named a specific moment he really noticed, the slow-motion catch, so it felt personal rather than automatic.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the 300 hearts compared with one comment?
qa.a: He may enjoy the hearts but take the one specific comment more seriously, since it shows someone paid attention.

grounding: Digital compliments are quick, so sincerity varies, and a specific personal message usually means more.

passage: So Devika, remember when Sir announced in assembly that my poem won the district round? Everybody turned and clapped. I was grinning like an idiot, but my hands went into my pockets and I looked at the floor. Then I said, loudly, "It was just luck, ask Devika, she gave me the rhyme." People laughed and Sir looked confused. After that I wanted to disappear. Later, in the corridor, Sir said quietly, "I meant it, Wasim. The last verse was really good." And that made my chest feel warm without anyone watching. I'm not against praise. I just can't take it with two hundred people looking. Can you tell them that next time?

qa.q: What did Sir announce in assembly?
qa.a: He announced that Wasim's poem won the district round.

qa.q: Why did Wasim joke and look at the floor when he was praised?
qa.a: He was pleased but uncomfortable being the centre of two hundred people's attention. The joke about luck may have been a way to deflect the attention, not a rejection of the praise.

qa.q: How could Sir give Wasim recognition next time?
qa.a: He could say a private word or write a short note, since the corridor comment felt warm to Wasim.

qa.q: How might Sir have read Wasim's joke in assembly?
qa.a: He may have thought Wasim did not care or was being modest, which is why he looked confused.

grounding: A teenager who is pleased by praise squirms in public, and a quiet private word suits better.

passage: I'm writing this because our class teacher asked us to observe something kind. During Friday's maths class, Ms Jain said, "Indu got the highest score and her method was very neat." Indu grinned for about a second, then rolled her eyes, pushed her notebook away and said, "Anyone could have done it." Her neck went red. The boys near me whistled and she laughed too loudly. I can't say what she felt, she might not like being noticed, or might have been shy. After class, Ms Jain quietly put a sticky note on her desk. Indu read it, folded it and tucked it into her pencil case, and she was smiling on the way out. Vaibhav.

qa.q: Who got the highest score in Friday's maths class?
qa.a: Indu got the highest score.

qa.q: What might Indu's red neck and eye-roll suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she felt pleased but self-conscious about being noticed in front of others. It could also be shyness, and Vaibhav says he cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Ms Jain do that seemed to work?
qa.a: She left a private sticky note on Indu's desk, which Indu kept and smiled about.

qa.q: How might the classmates who whistled see Indu's reaction?
qa.a: They may think she is enjoying the attention or does not care, though she may be squirming inside.

grounding: A teen looks pleased yet squirms at public praise, and a quiet private note suits better, seen by an observer.

passage: After choir practice Shalini caught Lalremsiami by the harmonium. "Your solo was amazing. Honestly the best thing I have ever heard in this school. You're a genius!" Lalremsiami said thanks and felt warm, and then Shalini added, "Can I copy your English notes tonight?" The warmth cooled a little. She thought about Mr Dutta, who had said the day before, "Your breath control on the long note has improved since August." That comment had named one thing and asked for nothing. "I can share the notes for one chapter," she said carefully. Shalini said, "Okay," cheerfully. Lalremsiami still didn't know for sure whether Shalini meant it. Perhaps she did, and had a request too.

qa.q: Where did Shalini catch Lalremsiami?
qa.a: She caught her by the harmonium after choir practice.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami's warm feeling cool after Shalini's request?
qa.a: She began to wonder if the big praise was leading up to the favour. She could not be sure, so she compared it with Mr Dutta's specific comment that asked for nothing.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami try next to understand Shalini's praise better?
qa.a: Notice whether Shalini's praise stays specific and continues when she asks for nothing, and keep her own answer about the notes calm and clear.

qa.q: How might Shalini see her own praise?
qa.a: She may honestly admire the solo and simply feel comfortable asking for notes.

grounding: Praise can be genuine, strategic or teasing, and the teen checks specificity and whether a request follows.

passage:
Dear Gopika didi,

You asked how the new class is going. Mostly fine, but I have a puzzle. A girl in my row, Esha, keeps saying things like, "You're the smartest person in the school, Sangeeta." I like hearing it, but I noticed she says it right before asking to borrow my pen, my notes or my seat. Meanwhile, my art teacher told me last week that my shading on the apple had gotten softer, and she asked me for nothing.

I don't want to be unfair to Esha, because I don't actually know her reasons. So I'm just watching whether her kind words show up when she doesn't need something. What do you think? 🤔

Love, Sangeeta

qa.q: Who says Sangeeta is the smartest person in the school?
qa.a: A girl in her row named Esha says it.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta hesitate to trust Esha's praise?
qa.a: She noticed the compliments come just before Esha asks to borrow something, so she wonders if the praise is a way to get a favour. She admits she does not know Esha's reasons.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do that is both fair and careful?
qa.a: Keep watching whether Esha's kindness appears when she needs nothing, and decide about lending her things calmly one at a time.

qa.q: How might Esha feel if she knew Sangeeta was watching her praise?
qa.a: She may feel misjudged if she meant it, or caught out if she did not.

grounding: A teenager compares specific, request-free praise with flattery and admits motives cannot be confirmed.

subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
passage: When I was in Class Ten, Jeevan, your grandmother's friend Meena told me something at the school bus stop, and her voice was flat. She said she had been saying to herself that she did not want to be here anymore. She made me promise not to tell anyone. I said yes, because I did not know what else to say. That night I could not eat. I knew a promise to a friend mattered, but I also knew this was too big for me. In the morning I told our class teacher, Mrs Rao, with shaking hands. Meena was angry for a week. Later she hugged me and said, "Thank you for not leaving me alone with it."

qa.q: Where did Meena tell the narrator her secret?
qa.a: She told it at the school bus stop.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling the night after she promised?
qa.a: She was frightened and troubled, so much that she could not eat. She knew the promise mattered, but she also saw the problem was too big to hold alone.

qa.q: What should a teenager do if a friend shares something this serious?
qa.a: Tell a trusted adult, such as a teacher or parent, soon, even if the friend asked for secrecy, and stay kind to the friend afterwards.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt when she found out the teacher knew?
qa.a: She may have felt betrayed and exposed for a while, and later relieved and cared for.

grounding: A teen recognises a worry as too big to hold and tells a trusted adult despite a promise of secrecy.

subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
passage: The power cut hit just as the evening rain got heavy. Vaibhav and Payal were sheltering at the bus stop, his phone at four percent. Payal was staring at the puddles. "Promise you won't tell anyone," she said. "My uncle's messages make me feel unsafe. He tells me not to say anything." Vaibhav's throat tightened. "Payal, I can't promise that. Someone has to know so you're safe." She cried a little. He typed a quick message to his mother, "I need to bring a friend home, it's about safety," and the phone died. They walked together through the rain, and the next morning he sat beside her in the counsellor's office and did not leave until she asked him to.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav's phone battery at the bus stop?
qa.a: His phone was at four percent.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav refuse to promise Payal that he would stay quiet?
qa.a: He felt that her safety mattered more than the secret, so a promise not to tell could have left her alone with the danger. His tightened throat shows he cared and was afraid for her.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that was helpful under pressure?
qa.a: He sent a message to his mother, stayed with Payal and went with her to the counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when he would not promise silence?
qa.a: She may have felt afraid or let down at first, and still glad that someone took it seriously.

grounding: A teenager tells a trusted adult about a safety worry even though a friend asked for secrecy.

passage:
Monday. Pradeep didn't get into the school band. He said, "It's fine," but his ears were red. Siddharth answered, "It's not a big deal, there's always next year." Pradeep looked away and said, "Yeah, right," and left early.

Wednesday. Siddharth couldn't stop thinking about Pradeep's face. He messaged, "That came out like your thing didn't matter. Sorry. Want to talk, or want me to just sit with you?" Pradeep replied, "Sit."

Saturday. They sat on the steps outside the music room. Pradeep talked about how much he'd practised. Siddharth said only, "That sounds really disappointing," and stayed. Pradeep leaned on the railing, breathing slowly, and finally said, "Thanks for staying."

qa.q: What did Pradeep not get into?
qa.a: He did not get into the school band.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep say "Yeah, right" and leave early on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and felt his disappointment was being brushed aside, since his ears were red and he looked away. He may also just have wanted to be alone.

qa.q: What worked better for Siddharth on Saturday than on Monday?
qa.a: Instead of offering a quick fix or calling it small, he listened, named the disappointment and stayed with Pradeep.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt after Pradeep left early?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and unsure, which is why he messaged to apologise on Wednesday.

grounding: A teenager comforts a friend by listening and staying, after minimising did not help.

passage: My grandson Hrithik asked me how to help a friend who was upset, so I told him about my school friend Tejas. I was your age then, Hrithik, and Tejas failed his board mathematics paper. I said all the clever things: "It's only one paper. You'll pass the supplementary." Tejas's jaw went hard and he stopped speaking to me for two days. I had answered the problem, not the person. So I went to his house with a small packet of jalebis and said, "I'm sorry. I'm here. You don't have to say anything." We sat on his verandah for an hour. He talked a little. Sometimes that's all it takes, just showing up and listening.

qa.q: What did Tejas fail?
qa.a: He failed his board mathematics paper.

qa.q: Why did Tejas stop speaking to his friend for two days?
qa.a: He felt brushed aside by clever comments, since his jaw went hard after hearing that it was only one paper. He probably wanted to feel understood first.

qa.q: What did the narrator change in his second visit?
qa.a: He apologised, stayed with Tejas and did not push him to talk, which let Tejas open up a little.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when his friend came with jalebis?
qa.a: He may have felt cared for and less alone, because his friend showed up without trying to fix everything.

grounding: An elder recalls that fixing or minimising felt dismissive to a friend, and listening and presence helped.
